etymology: American academic legal theory originating at Harvard Law School in the late 1970s and codified at a 1989 workshop in Madison, Wisconsin (Crenshaw, Delgado, Bell, Matsuda). The phrase "critical" carries the Frankfurt-School Marxist sense of critique-of-power-structures; the phrase "race theory" identifies race as the primary analytical category for that critique.
biblical_def: Critical Race Theory (CRT) is a post-Marxist American academic framework that reframes society as an organized system of racial oppression in which whiteness operates as a power-structure of unearned privilege and non-whiteness as a position of structural oppression. Its defining moves: race is socially constructed but politically real; racism is systemic, not merely individual; ordinary individuals' subjective intent is largely irrelevant compared to disparate outcomes; the Enlightenment categories of merit, neutrality, and objectivity are themselves white-supremacist constructs; the lived experience of the oppressed has epistemic privilege; and the only legitimate posture for whites is sustained anti-racist activism. CRT entered American evangelical institutions through the late 2010s (Resolution 9 at the 2019 Southern Baptist Convention; books by Tisby, McCaulley, McKissic; programs at major Evangelical seminaries) and was decisively rejected at the 2021 SBC after sustained Reformed-confessional pushback. From the Reformed-confessional standpoint, CRT is a competing anthropology that displaces the biblical categories of sin (Rom 5:12, all in Adam), redemption (Gal 3:28, one in Christ), and the heart (Jer 17:9) with the framework's race-as-master-category. It is rejected on biblical grounds, not on political grounds.
webster_summary: American post-Marxist academic framework treating race as the master analytical category for society; codified 1989; entered evangelical institutions late 2010s; rejected at 2021 SBC after Reformed pushback; a competing anthropology displacing the biblical categories of sin, redemption, and the heart.

Decisively rejected by the 2021 Southern Baptist Convention; rejected on biblical-anthropological grounds by Reformed-confessional Christianity.

corruption_summary: CRT is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names. The entry exists to identify the framework, name its representatives, and rebut it on biblical-anthropological grounds.
corruption_paragraphs: Competing anthropology. CRT proposes a different fundamental account of what human beings are than Scripture does. Scripture: all humans descend from one couple (Acts 17:26); all share original sin (Rom 5:12); all who are in Christ are one (Gal 3:28). CRT: humans are constituted by their racial position within a power structure; the master analytical category for human relations is race-based oppression; subjective unity in Christ is decentered in favor of structural analysis of who is racially oppressor vs oppressed. These are not complementary frameworks. They are competing answers to the question 'what is a human being?' The Reformed reader rejects the competing answer. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this entry rebuts CRT; banned-register terms appear here as named-corruption discussion.

Epistemic privilege of lived experience. CRT teaches that the oppressed have epistemic privilege over the oppressors — that they see what the privileged class cannot see. From the Reformed standpoint, this directly contradicts Jer 17:9 and Rom 3:10-18: every human heart, regardless of social position, is deceitful and unable to know itself rightly without divine illumination. The oppressed do not have epistemic privilege; only the Spirit-given mind of Christ does (1 Cor 2:14-16). Lived experience is not an alternative ground of theological authority. The closed canon is.

etymology: Modern (post-1970s) Western Christian movement reinterpreting the biblical passages on sexuality so that monogamous same-sex sexual unions and (more recently) gender-identity-altering interventions are presented as morally permissible and capable of receiving the blessing of the church. The label "affirming" was chosen by the movement itself to mean "affirming of LGBTQ identities and unions."
biblical_def: Affirming theology is the modern Western Christian movement that reinterprets the canonical biblical passages on sexuality — Lev 18:22 and 20:13, Rom 1:18-32, 1 Cor 6:9-11, 1 Tim 1:9-10 — so as to permit (and more recently, bless) monogamous same-sex sexual unions and to validate gender-identity claims detached from biological sex. Major representatives include Matthew Vines (God and the Gay Christian, 2014), Ken Wilson (A Letter to My Congregation, 2014), James Brownson (Bible, Gender, Sexuality, 2013), David Gushee, and the institutional shift of the United Methodist Church split (2022-2024), the Episcopal Church earlier, the PCUSA earlier, and the Reformed Church in America. The exegetical moves common across affirming proposals: Leviticus addresses cultic / Canaanite-religion practices, not consensual love; Romans 1 condemns excess and lust, not orientation; the <em>arsenokoitai</em> and <em>malakoi</em> of 1 Cor 6 mean something narrower than contemporary same-sex unions; the genuine biblical pattern (covenanted faithful love) is fulfilled in committed same-sex marriages. From the Reformed-confessional standpoint, every move is rebutted on the plain reading of the canonical text in its Mosaic, prophetic, dominical, and apostolic continuity. The dictionary holds the historic Christian position: monogamous one-man-one-woman marriage is the only category of legitimate sexual union, and same-sex sexual acts are sin regardless of relational frame. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this entry names and rebuts affirming theology.

corruption_summary: Affirming theology is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names and rebuts. The entry exists to identify the framework, name its representatives, summarize its exegetical moves, and rebut each move on the plain reading of the canonical text.
corruption_paragraphs: Cultic-Canaanite reframing of Lev 18. Affirming readers (Vines, Brownson) propose that Lev 18:22 addresses ancient Near Eastern cultic / Canaanite-religion male prostitution, not consensual same-sex unions. The plain reading rebuts: the surrounding chapter prohibits adultery, incest, child-sacrifice, and bestiality — all moral categories transcending cultic context; the same prohibition appears again at Lev 20:13 with capital sentence; the Pentateuchal pattern treats sex-acts categorically, not cultically; and the New Testament treats the prohibition as continuing moral law (Rom 1, 1 Cor 6, 1 Tim 1).

Excess-not-orientation reframing of Romans 1. Affirming readers (Wilson) propose that Rom 1:26-27 addresses excessive, idolatrous, or non-covenanted same-sex lust, not committed-monogamous same-sex unions. The plain reading rebuts: Paul's argument from creation (Rom 1:20) and from nature (1:26 'natural use,' 1:27 'against nature') grounds his rebuke in the created order of Gen 1:27 male-female complementarity, not in any extra-text qualifier about commitment or excess. The 'natural use' is the male-female complementarity of creation; the 'against nature' is its violation regardless of relational frame. To find a relational-frame qualifier in Rom 1 is to import it from outside the text. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph rebuts the affirming reading of Rom 1.

etymology: Academic theological subfield originating in the late 1980s and early 1990s, applying queer theory (Butler, Sedgwick, Foucault) to biblical and theological texts. The term "queer" in the academic sense includes deliberate destabilization of binary categories, not just gay-and-lesbian identity politics.
biblical_def: Queer theology is the academic theological subfield that applies queer theory — a 1990s Butler / Sedgwick / Foucault framework that deliberately destabilizes binary categories (male / female, heterosexual / homosexual, normal / deviant) — to biblical interpretation and Christian theology. It is distinct from (and more radical than) affirming theology. Major representatives: Marcella Althaus-Reid (Indecent Theology, 2000), Patrick Cheng (Radical Love, 2011), Robert Goss, Linn Marie Tonstad. Where affirming theology argues that committed-monogamous same-sex unions can fit within the existing biblical framework, queer theology argues that the framework itself is the problem — that the creational binaries of Gen 1:27 are oppressive social constructions that the gospel destabilizes, that Jesus himself is queer (Cheng's central claim), that the church should embrace fluidity over fixity in every category from gender to family to theology. From the Reformed-confessional standpoint, queer theology is rebutted at the foundation: Gen 1:27 establishes the male-female creational binary as the imago Dei structure of humanity; Christ's incarnation as the male Son of Mary (Matt 1:25; Luke 1:31; Luke 2:21) consecrates rather than destabilizes biological sex; and the apostolic Lord's words at Matt 19:4-6 ground all sexual ethics in the creational binary. The dictionary holds the historic Christian position categorically. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this entry names and rebuts queer theology.
webster_summary: Academic theological subfield (since late 1980s) applying queer theory to biblical interpretation; more radical than affirming theology in that it rejects the underlying biblical framework rather than reinterpreting it; representatives Althaus-Reid, Cheng, Goss, Tonstad; rebutted from Gen 1:27 + Matt 19:4-6.

corruption_summary: Queer theology is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names and rebuts. It is more radical than affirming theology in that it rejects the creational binary rather than reinterpreting biblical sexuality within it.
corruption_paragraphs: Destabilizing the creational binary. Queer theology's defining move is to treat the male-female binary of Gen 1:27 as itself an oppressive social construct rather than as the imago Dei structure of humanity. The plain reading of Gen 1:27, reinforced by Christ's appeal to it at Matt 19:4-6, rebuts the framing: the male-female binary is given, embodied, image-of-God, and creational, not contingent or culturally constructed. The Lord's appeal to Genesis to settle the divorce question is the apostolic-canonical pattern for settling any sexuality question. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph rebuts queer theology's destabilization of the creational binary.

Christ as queer. Patrick Cheng's Radical Love proposes that Christ himself is queer because Christ destabilizes categories (Jew / Gentile, slave / free, male / female) per Gal 3:28. The proposal collapses two distinct claims: (a) Christ relativizes some social categories with respect to salvation (Jew/Gentile, slave/free; Gal 3:28's pre-resurrection list); (b) Christ destabilizes the creational male-female binary (Cheng's queer claim). The Reformed reader: the gospel relativizes the social categories of position; it does not relativize the creational categories of sex. Gal 3:28's 'neither male nor female' addresses the position-before-God of those in Christ, not the embodied creational structure of humanity (Eph 5:22-33 written by the same apostle explicitly maintains the husband-wife, male-female structure within the gospel).

etymology: Term coined by sociologist Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton in Soul Searching: The Religious and Spiritual Lives of American Teenagers (Oxford, 2005) to describe the de facto religion of American adolescents as revealed in the National Study of Youth and Religion (2001-2005). The label has since become the standard sociological-theological term for the religion of much of contemporary American Christianity, not just adolescents.
biblical_def: Moralistic Therapeutic Deism (MTD) is the de facto religion of much of contemporary American Christianity, named by Christian Smith from the 2001-2005 National Study of Youth and Religion. Smith summarized its five tenets: (1) a God exists who created the world and watches over human life; (2) God wants people to be good, nice, and fair to each other, as taught in the Bible and most world religions; (3) the central goal of life is to be happy and feel good about oneself; (4) God is not particularly involved in one's life except when needed to resolve a problem; (5) good people go to heaven when they die. As Smith observed, this is not historic Christianity. It is a deistic background-God plus therapeutic self-actualization plus a vague moralism, with no place for sin, the cross, the Spirit, the church, the second coming, or any of the doctrinal substance of Reformed-confessional Christianity. The label MTD became immediately useful because Smith documented that it had displaced historic Christianity as the operative religion of most American Protestant teenagers (and, by extension, the operative religion of much of seeker-sensitive American Evangelicalism that shaped them). The Reformed reader receives MTD as a thorough diagnosis: the contemporary therapeutic register has substituted for the gospel and must be replaced by recovered Reformed-confessional Christianity. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: this entry uses 'therapeutic' to describe the corruption pattern Smith named.
webster_summary: Five-point de facto religion of contemporary American Christianity, named by Christian Smith (2005): deistic background-God + therapeutic self-actualization + vague moralism; displaces historic Christianity's doctrines of sin, the cross, the Spirit, the church.

corruption_summary: MTD is itself the corruption pattern being named. The entry exists to identify the five-point diagnosis as Smith offered it, document its displacement of historic Christianity, and prescribe Reformed-confessional recovery.
corruption_paragraphs: Substitution for historic Christianity. MTD shares vocabulary with Christianity (God, Bible, heaven, prayer) but has substituted radically different content. The God of MTD is deistic and uninvolved (not the LORD of covenant who speaks, redeems, judges, dwells). The Bible of MTD is moral advice (not the inspired, inerrant Word that pierces to dividing soul and spirit, Heb 4:12). Heaven in MTD is the destination of good people (not the eternal communion of those who have been washed in the blood of the Lamb). The substitution is so thorough that an entire generation of American Protestant teenagers grew up assuming MTD was Christianity; the recovery requires explicit Reformed-confessional teaching, not vague spirituality.

Therapeutic register substitution. MTD's third tenet — the central goal of life is to be happy and feel good about oneself — is the displacement of the Westminster Shorter Catechism's first answer: man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him forever. The two answers are not complementary; they are competing summaries of human telos. Reformed-confessional recovery from MTD requires recovering the doxological-doctrinal frame in which the soul's true peace and joy are found in the worship of God, not in the affirmation of the self. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: 'therapeutic register' is named here as the corruption pattern.

etymology: Term coined in late-18th-century German biblical scholarship to distinguish "lower" or textual criticism (manuscript-collation; legitimate work) from "higher" criticism (questions of authorship, date, sources, composition; the academic method the dictionary rebuts). The term höhere Kritik is associated with Johann Eichhorn (1780s).
biblical_def: Higher criticism is the academic method that approaches the biblical text with the working assumption that its claims about authorship, date, sources, composition, and historicity may be revised on naturalistic-historical grounds against the canonical claims. Originating in the German Aufklärung (Enlightenment) of the late 18th century — Eichhorn, Reimarus, Lessing, then de Wette, F.C. Baur, Wellhausen, Bultmann — it produced the now-standard academic theories that the Reformed-confessional reader rejects: documentary hypothesis (JEDP) for the Pentateuch, denying Mosaic authorship; multiple-Isaiah theory; late dating of Daniel (second century BC after the prophesied events); rejection of Pauline authorship of the Pastoral Epistles; mythological-versus-historical readings of the Gospels; the quest of the historical Jesus that denies the supernatural elements of the canonical record. The method's defining move is that the canonical text's self-witness about itself (Moses wrote, Isaiah wrote, Daniel wrote, Paul wrote) is replaced by the modern academic reconstruction. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the canonical self-witness is authoritative because the canonical text is the inspired Word of God (2 Tim 3:16); the academic-critical reconstruction is human conjecture against divine testimony. The dictionary's authorship convictions (single Isaiah; sixth-century Daniel; Pauline authorship of all 13 epistles; Mosaic Pentateuch; apostolic Gospels) are the historic Christian position from the apostolic age through Calvin and the Reformers, and are held against the higher-critical reconstruction. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this entry rebuts higher criticism by name.
webster_summary: Late-18th-century German academic method approaching the biblical text with naturalistic-historical assumptions against canonical claims; produces JEDP, multiple-Isaiah, late-Daniel, deutero-Pauline theories; rebutted from canonical self-witness + 2 Tim 3:16 inspired-Word doctrine.
webster_full: HIGHER CRITICISM, noun phrase. German Aufklärung biblical method, late 18th century onward.

Major theorists: Eichhorn (1780s); Reimarus and Lessing; de Wette; F.C. Baur (Tübingen school); Julius Wellhausen (documentary hypothesis, 1878); Rudolf Bultmann (form criticism, demythologization).
Major outputs: JEDP documentary hypothesis; multiple-Isaiah theory; second-century-BC Daniel; deutero-Pauline Pastoral Epistles; quest of the historical Jesus.
Rebutted from canonical self-witness + verbal-plenary inspiration of Scripture (2 Tim 3:16; 2 Pet 1:21).

corruption_summary: Higher criticism is itself the corruption pattern being named. The entry exists to identify the method, name its representatives, document its standard outputs, and rebut it from the canonical self-witness plus the verbal-plenary inspiration of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Naturalistic assumption against canonical self-witness. Higher criticism's defining move is the methodological commitment that the biblical text's claims about itself must be evaluated by naturalistic-historical reconstruction rather than received as authoritative. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the canonical self-witness IS the data; the academic reconstruction is the conjecture. Moses wrote the Pentateuch because the Pentateuch (and the Lord Jesus at Mark 12:26, John 5:46-47, Luke 24:44) says he did. Isaiah wrote Isaiah because Isaiah and the Lord Jesus (Matt 13:14-15 citing Isa 6, etc.) say he did. The methodological assumption that the text's self-witness must yield to academic reconstruction is the corruption pattern. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this paragraph rebuts the higher-critical methodological assumption.

Wellhausen's documentary hypothesis specifically. The most famous higher-critical product, Julius Wellhausen's 1878 reconstruction of the Pentateuch as four post-Mosaic sources (J, E, D, P), was decisively criticized within secular academic Old Testament studies in the late 20th century (the work of Whybray, Rendtorff, the so-called 'collapse of the documentary hypothesis' in the 1980s-2000s), and continues to be defended only in soft / minimalist forms. The Reformed-confessional reader notes both that the historic Christian position (Mosaic authorship) was right all along, and that secular academic biblical studies' own internal criticism eventually corroborated this from the inside. Higher criticism's confidence in its own results has been chastened by its own intra-disciplinary history.

etymology: Standard label for the higher-critical reconstruction of the Pentateuch as a composite of four post-Mosaic sources: the Yahwist (J, from German Jahwist), the Elohist (E), the Deuteronomist (D), and the Priestly source (P). Codified by Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels (Berlin, 1878).
biblical_def: The documentary hypothesis is the central output of 19th-century German higher criticism of the Pentateuch — the theory that Genesis through Deuteronomy is not a unified Mosaic composition but a redaction of four post-Mosaic source-documents (J, E, D, P) compiled over roughly seven centuries (c. 10th to 5th century BC) by successive editors. Julius Wellhausen's 1878 Prolegomena codified the standard form; the theory became the dominant academic position for nearly a century. The Reformed-confessional position holds Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch on the canonical self-witness (Exod 17:14; 24:4; 34:27; Num 33:2; Deut 31:9, 24-26) and on the Lord Jesus's own attribution (Mark 12:26 'in the book of Moses'; John 5:46-47 'Moses... wrote of me'; Luke 24:44 'in the law of Moses'). It rejects JEDP on three grounds: (1) the canonical self-witness is authoritative; (2) the criteria by which JEDP was constructed (different divine names, supposed doublets, supposed contradictions) have been internally criticized within secular academic Old Testament studies since the 1970s, and many specialists now regard the classical hypothesis as collapsed; (3) the late dates Wellhausen assigned to the P source for theological reasons have been refuted by archaeological discoveries (Hittite treaty parallels for Deuteronomy; Late Bronze Age tabernacle materials; etc.) since World War II. The dictionary rejects JEDP on biblical, intra-academic, and archaeological grounds. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this entry rebuts JEDP by name.
webster_summary: Central 19th-century higher-critical theory of the Pentateuch as a composite of four post-Mosaic sources (J, E, D, P); codified by Wellhausen 1878; rebutted by canonical self-witness + Lord Jesus's attribution + intra-academic collapse since the 1970s + archaeological refutation of late dating.
webster_full: DOCUMENTARY HYPOTHESIS (JEDP), noun phrase. Central output of 19th-century German higher criticism.
Theory: Pentateuch composed of four post-Mosaic source documents — Yahwist (J), Elohist (E), Deuteronomist (D), Priestly (P) — redacted over roughly the 10th to 5th centuries BC.
Codified: Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels (Berlin, 1878).

Status: Dominant academic position from c. 1880 to c. 1970; internal academic criticism (Whybray, Rendtorff, Van Seters, the 'collapse of the documentary hypothesis') has eroded the classical hypothesis since the 1970s; no replacement consensus has emerged.
Rejected by the dictionary on biblical, intra-academic, and archaeological grounds; Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch is the dictionary's confessional position.

corruption_summary: The documentary hypothesis is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names and rebuts. The Pentateuch is the work of Moses, attested by the canonical self-witness and by the Lord Jesus's own attribution, against the late-19th-century academic reconstruction.
corruption_paragraphs: Canonical self-witness over academic reconstruction. The Pentateuch repeatedly identifies Moses as its author or as the recipient of its commands to write (Exod 17:14; 24:4; 34:27; Num 33:2; Deut 31:9, 24-26). The Lord Jesus repeatedly attributes the Pentateuch to Moses (Mark 12:26; John 5:46-47; Luke 24:44). The apostle Paul does the same (Rom 10:5). The choice between JEDP and Mosaic authorship is not the choice between two scholarly hypotheses; it is the choice between trusting Wellhausen's 1878 reconstruction and trusting the Lord Jesus's stated assumption. The dictionary chooses the Lord Jesus's stated assumption. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this paragraph rebuts JEDP on its merits.

Intra-academic collapse since the 1970s. The classical Wellhausen hypothesis has been increasingly criticized within secular academic Old Testament studies for fifty years. R.N. Whybray (The Making of the Pentateuch, 1987) demonstrated that the criteria by which JEDP was constructed (different divine names, supposed doublets, supposed contradictions) do not in fact support the four-source partition. Rolf Rendtorff and John Van Seters proposed major revisions or replacements. The current academic state is one of dispersed micro-hypotheses without consensus; the classical confidence of 1878 to 1970 has eroded. The Reformed-confessional reader notes that this internal academic collapse corroborates from the inside what the apostolic-Lord's-attribution had said all along.

etymology: Modern Protestant movement originating in late-18th-century Germany (Schleiermacher, Lessing) and reaching full institutional dominance in the early-20th-century American mainline churches. The term "liberal" carries the post-Enlightenment sense of "free from constraint by traditional authority," not the contemporary American political sense.
biblical_def: Theological liberalism is the modern Protestant movement that revises historic Christian doctrine to make it compatible with post-Enlightenment naturalism, modern science, and modern moral sensibility. Originating with Friedrich Schleiermacher (On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers, 1799; The Christian Faith, 1821-22), developed by Albrecht Ritschl, Adolf von Harnack (What Is Christianity?, 1900), and Walter Rauschenbusch (Social Gospel), it reached full institutional dominance in the American mainline Protestant churches by roughly 1920-1930 and provoked the great fundamentalist-modernist controversy of the 1920s. Its defining moves: doctrine is reduced to ethics or to religious feeling; miracles are denied or reinterpreted naturalistically; the deity of Christ is denied or recast (Christ as the supreme religious teacher rather than the eternal Son incarnate); substitutionary atonement is replaced by exemplarist or moral-influence theories; biblical inerrancy is denied; the historic creeds are revised or abandoned. J. Gresham Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923) made the decisive Reformed-confessional argument: liberalism is not a variant of Christianity but a different religion that uses Christian vocabulary. The dictionary holds Machen's verdict. The 20th-century American mainline Protestant decline (the so-called "empty mainline pews") is the empirical confirmation of Machen's diagnosis. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this entry rebuts theological liberalism by name.
webster_summary: Modern Protestant movement (Schleiermacher onward) revising historic Christian doctrine to fit post-Enlightenment naturalism; dominant in early-20th-century American mainline; diagnosed by J. Decisive Reformed-confessional rebuttal: J. Gresham Machen, Christianity and Liberalism (1923) — liberalism is not a variant of Christianity but a different religion.

corruption_summary: Theological liberalism is itself the corruption pattern being named. The entry exists to identify the movement's founders, document its defining moves, and rebut it via Machen's 1923 verdict and the empirical 20th-century mainline decline.
corruption_paragraphs: Christian vocabulary, different religion. Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923) made the decisive argument: liberalism uses words like God, Christ, salvation, gospel, atonement, and Bible, but its content for each word is so different from historic Christianity's content that it constitutes a different religion. Liberalism's God is immanent rather than transcendent-and-immanent; its Christ is the supreme moral example rather than the eternal Son incarnate; its salvation is moral self-improvement under divine encouragement rather than imputed righteousness through faith alone; its gospel is the brotherhood of humanity under the fatherhood of God; its atonement is moral influence; its Bible is the religious testimony of an evolving community. Each of these is the substitution of a modern philosophical content for the historic Christian content of the same word.

Mainline decline as empirical confirmation. The 20th-century American mainline Protestant decline is the empirical history of liberalism's diagnosis. The mainline denominations that embraced theological liberalism most fully (PCUSA, ECUSA, UMC, ELCA, DOC) have hemorrhaged membership for roughly seventy years, while confessionally conservative Reformed-evangelical communions (PCA, OPC, SBC pre-2020, EPC, ARP) have either grown or held steady. The pattern is so consistent that secular sociologists of religion have made it a textbook case. Empirical confirmation of Machen's 1923 prediction: a movement that surrenders the doctrinal substance of historic Christianity cannot sustain itself for long, because the doctrinal substance is precisely what the gospel is.

etymology: Term coined by C. Peter Wagner (Fuller Seminary missiologist) in the late 1990s and early 2000s to describe what he claimed was a global Spirit-led restoration of the offices of apostle and prophet to the present-day church. The label was Wagner's own; he proposed it as a Second Reformation.
biblical_def: The New Apostolic Reformation (NAR) is the contemporary charismatic movement, coined and theorized by C. Peter Wagner (1930-2016), that claims the Holy Spirit is restoring the offices of apostle and prophet to the present-day church and that these new apostles and prophets carry the same authority their first-century counterparts did. Major streams within or adjacent to NAR include the International House of Prayer (IHOP, Mike Bickle, Kansas City), Bethel Church (Bill Johnson, Redding, California), Jesus Culture, Global Spheres (Wagner himself), and the Seven Mountains Mandate (Lance Wallnau, Loren Cunningham). Its theological distinctives: continuing canonical-level apostolic authority; ongoing prophetic words equal in weight to Scripture; signs-and-wonders evangelism; transferable spiritual anointings; dominionist eschatology (the church is to bring the kingdom by taking the seven mountains of culture); strategic-level spiritual warfare (territorial spirits, generational curses). The Reformed-confessional position rejects NAR on cessationist grounds: the apostolic office was foundational and unique (Eph 2:20; Acts 1:21-22's apostle-requirements that no living person can meet); the canon is closed (Heb 1:1-2; Jude 1:3 'the faith which was once delivered'); ongoing prophetic words equal to Scripture undermine *sola Scriptura*; signs-and-wonders are not the apostolic-canonical pattern for normal church life. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: 'dominionist' here names a NAR position, not a generic accusation.

corruption_paragraphs: Restored-apostolic-authority claim. NAR's defining move is that present-day persons carry the same apostolic authority the original Twelve and Paul did. The plain New Testament data rebut: Acts 1:21-22 specifies that an apostle must have companied with the Lord Jesus from his baptism through his resurrection-witness, a requirement no living person can meet; Eph 2:20 specifies that the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, foundational and therefore non-repeatable; Heb 1:1-2 specifies that God's prior-prophetic speaking has been completed in the Son. The closed canon is the rule for the present age; the apostolic office is not restored because it was a one-time foundational office.

Sola Scriptura undermined by ongoing prophetic words. NAR's secondary distinctive is that present-day prophetic words carry quasi-canonical authority for the body. Mike Bickle's IHOP and Bill Johnson's Bethel both teach that current prophetic words must be received and acted on. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: every present-day word is subject to the closed canon (1 Cor 14:29 'let the other judge'; 1 Thess 5:21 'prove all things'), and any present-day word that adds to, contradicts, or overrides Scripture is not from God (Rev 22:18-19). Mike Bickle's documented decades-long pattern of prophetic words later falsified or revised, and Bill Johnson's documented teachings on Christ's kenotic incarnation (Christ ministering as 'a man in right relationship with God,' allegedly equivalent to any believer) and on signs-and-wonders as evidence of the kingdom, both fall under the closed-canon judgment. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph rebuts NAR's revelation-claims by name.

etymology: 20th-century American theological movement applying Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy (Process and Reality, 1929) to the doctrine of God. Major theological codifier: Charles Hartshorne (Whitehead's protege; The Divine Relativity, 1948).
biblical_def: Process theology is the 20th-century American theological movement that applies Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy to the doctrine of God, producing a deity radically different from classical Reformed-confessional theism. Major representatives: Charles Hartshorne (The Divine Relativity, 1948); John B. Cobb Jr. (Claremont School of Theology); David Ray Griffin; Schubert Ogden. Process theology's God is dipolar — with a primordial (abstract, unchanging) nature AND a consequent (concrete, changing, world-affected) nature. God is not omniscient in the classical sense (the future is open even to God because the future is not yet actual); God is not omnipotent in the classical sense (God lures rather than determines); God is not immutable (God genuinely changes in response to the world); God is not impassible (God genuinely suffers with the world); divine action is persuasive and non-coercive. From the Reformed-confessional standpoint, process theology rejects the classical attributes (aseity, immutability, impassibility, divine simplicity, omniscience, omnipotence) at every point and constructs a finite God who is neither the God of Scripture nor the God of any historic Christian confession. Open Theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) is a closer-to-Evangelical descendant that adopts process theology's openness of the future and limitation of divine knowledge while attempting to maintain more of the classical framework. The dictionary rejects process theology categorically and open theism as a more pastoral-sounding variant of the same error. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this entry rebuts process theology and open theism by name.
webster_summary: 20th-century American theological movement applying Whitehead's process philosophy to God; produces a dipolar, changing, finite deity; major representatives Hartshorne, Cobb, Griffin; rejected at every point by classical Reformed theism (aseity, immutability, impassibility, omniscience, omnipotence).
webster_full: PROCESS THEOLOGY, noun phrase. 20th-century American movement applying Whitehead's process philosophy to God.
Philosophical source: Alfred North Whitehead, Process and Reality (Gifford Lectures 1927-28, published 1929).
Theological codifier: Charles Hartshorne, The Divine Relativity (1948); The Logic of Perfection (1962).
Other major figures: John B. Cobb Jr. (Claremont); David Ray Griffin; Schubert Ogden; Marjorie Suchocki.
Adjacent Evangelical-facing descendant: Open Theism (Clark Pinnock, Greg Boyd, John Sanders).
Rejected at every point by classical Reformed-confessional theism.

corruption_summary: Process theology is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names and rebuts. The entry exists to identify Whitehead's philosophical source, Hartshorne's theological codification, the resulting attribute-by-attribute departure from classical Reformed theism, and the Open-Theist descendant.
corruption_paragraphs: Attribute-by-attribute departure from classical theism. Process theology denies divine aseity (God's life depends on relation to the world); divine immutability (God changes); divine impassibility (God suffers); exhaustive divine foreknowledge (the future is open); divine omnipotence in the classical sense (God lures rather than determines); divine simplicity (God is dipolar). Each of these denials contradicts an explicit Scriptural assertion: Mal 3:6 ('I am the LORD, I change not'); Isa 46:10 ('My counsel shall stand'); Ps 139:1-6 (exhaustive foreknowledge of every word); Eph 1:11 ('worketh all things after the counsel of his own will'). The classical Reformed attributes are not a Greek-philosophical overlay on the biblical text; they are the biblical text's own theology stated in technical vocabulary. To deny them at every point is to construct a different God.

Open Theism as Evangelical-facing variant. Clark Pinnock, Greg Boyd, and John Sanders proposed an Evangelical-facing variant of process theology under the name Open Theism: God is genuinely affected by the world, the future is partly open even to God, divine action is partly responsive and partly determinate. Open Theism attempts to preserve more of the classical framework than full process theology does, presents itself as biblically motivated (Hosea's grieving God; Genesis 6:6 'it repented the LORD'; Numbers 23:19 supposedly reconciled by anthropomorphism), and has been more pastorally appealing to Evangelicals than full process theology has been. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the same Scriptures Open Theism cites for divine responsiveness (Hosea, Gen 6, Jonah) are exactly the Scriptures that classical theism has handled with the doctrine of accommodation and anthropomorphism for two thousand years. Open Theism offers nothing exegetically new; what it offers is a different God.

etymology: Mid-20th-century American sociological category for the seven historic American Protestant denominations institutionally dominant from the 19th century through approximately World War II: the United Methodist Church (UMC), the Presbyterian Church USA (PCUSA), the Episcopal Church (TEC / ECUSA), the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA), the American Baptist Churches USA (ABCUSA), the United Church of Christ (UCC), and the Disciples of Christ (DOC). "Mainline" originally referred to the wealthy Philadelphia Main Line suburbs where many of these denominations' members concentrated.
biblical_def: Mainline Protestantism is the institutional category for the seven historic American Protestant denominations — UMC, PCUSA, TEC, ELCA, ABCUSA, UCC, DOC — that were institutionally dominant in American Protestant Christianity from the 19th century through World War II, and that adopted theological liberalism (Schleiermacher-onward, q.v.) at the institutional level over the early-to-mid 20th century, becoming the "mainline" that historic Christianity left. The defining 20th-century pattern is consistent across all seven: institutional adoption of higher-critical biblical scholarship; denial of biblical inerrancy in confessional statements; ordination of women (UMC 1956, PCUSA 1956, TEC 1976, ELCA 1970); ordination of openly practicing gay clergy (TEC 1989 first openly-gay priest; ECUSA's Gene Robinson 2003; ELCA 2009; PCUSA 2011; UMC split 2022-2024); blessing of same-sex unions; replacement of historic Trinitarian liturgical language with inclusive-language formulas. The empirical history is striking: each of the seven mainline denominations has lost roughly half its membership since 1965-1975, while confessionally conservative Reformed-evangelical denominations have either grown or held steady over the same period. The dictionary names the mainline as the institutional embodiment of theological liberalism's century-long arc and as the empirical confirmation of J. Gresham Machen's 1923 diagnosis. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this entry names mainline Protestantism's adopted theology and its empirical institutional decline.

corruption_summary: Mainline Protestantism as a category is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names: the seven historic American Protestant denominations that institutionally embodied theological liberalism over the 20th century and now exemplify its consequences.
corruption_paragraphs: Institutional adoption of liberalism. The 20th-century history of each mainline denomination follows the same arc: 1900-1930, institutional adoption of higher-critical biblical scholarship; 1930-1960, removal of inerrancy from confessional statements; 1956-1976, ordination of women; 1989-2024, ordination of openly practicing gay clergy and blessing of same-sex unions; 1990-present, inclusive-language liturgies replacing historic Trinitarian formulas. The arc is so consistent across institutionally independent denominations that it constitutes a sociological-theological pattern: liberalism's working-out at institutional scale takes roughly a century and produces predictable downstream changes.

Empirical decline as confirmation of Machen. Every mainline denomination has lost approximately half its membership since the peak years of 1965-1975 (PCUSA from c. 4.2M to c. 1.1M as of 2023; UMC from c. 11M to c. 5.7M before the 2022-2024 split; TEC from c. 3.4M to c. 1.5M; UCC from c. 2M to c. 700K; etc.). Over the same period, confessionally conservative Reformed-evangelical communions (PCA, OPC, EPC, ARP, conservative SBC, Bible churches) have either grown or held steady. The empirical pattern confirms Machen's 1923 prediction: a movement that surrenders the doctrinal substance of historic Christianity cannot long sustain itself. The mainline is the case study. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph names the empirical decline of mainline Protestantism without softening.

etymology: Named for Charles Grandison Finney (1792-1875), the American Second-Great-Awakening evangelist and later president of Oberlin College, whose methodological and theological innovations (the anxious bench, protracted meetings, the altar call, decisional regeneration, semi-Pelagian soteriology) shaped American revivalism from roughly 1830 onward. The term "Finneyism" is used by Reformed-confessional critics to mark the package of Finney's methodological and doctrinal innovations as a coherent departure from historic Reformed soteriology and ecclesiology.
biblical_def: Finneyism is the package of methodological and doctrinal innovations Charles Grandison Finney (1792-1875) introduced into American revivalism during the Second Great Awakening (c. 1820-1850) and that continue to shape American evangelicalism's altar-call and decisional-regeneration culture. Methodologically: the "new measures" including the anxious bench (a designated front-row seat for those under conviction), protracted meetings (consecutive nightly meetings designed to produce conversions), the altar call (public invitation to come forward as the act of conversion itself), and use of women in mixed public preaching. Theologically: explicit rejection of the historic Reformed doctrine of total depravity (Finney held a Pelagian-tinged ability of the natural man to choose Christ); rejection of substitutionary penal atonement in favor of a moral-government theory; rejection of justification by imputed righteousness in favor of governmental justification; rejection of original sin as imputed. Finney's Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835) and Systematic Theology (1846, revised 1851) are the primary sources. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal was articulated by Charles Hodge, J.W. Nevin, and most decisively in the 20th century by Iain Murray (Revival and Revivalism, 1994). The dictionary holds that Finney's theological innovations are Pelagian and that his methodological innovations (especially the altar call and decisional regeneration) have produced a century and a half of American Evangelicalism that confuses public response with regenerate conversion. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: 'Pelagian' here names a specific historic position, not a generic accusation.

corruption_summary: Finneyism is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names: Charles G. Finney's methodological and doctrinal innovations rejected the historic Reformed soteriology and produced the altar-call and decisional-regeneration culture that has shaped American Evangelicalism since 1830.
corruption_paragraphs: Pelagian-tinged soteriology against the historic Reformed position. Finney's Systematic Theology (1846) explicitly rejected total depravity in the classical Reformed sense, holding that the natural man retains the moral ability to choose Christ if his motives are sufficiently moved. This is Pelagian on the Reformed reading (the historic Western-church verdict at the Council of Carthage 418 and Second Council of Orange 529 condemned exactly this position). The biblical rebuttal: Eph 2:1-5 (dead in trespasses); John 6:44 (no man can come except the Father draw him); John 1:13 (born not of the will of man but of God); Rom 9:16 (not of him that willeth). The historic Reformed soteriology Finney explicitly rejected is the historic biblical soteriology.

Methodological altar-call innovation. The altar call — the public invitation to come forward as the act of conversion itself — is a Finney-introduced innovation not present in the New Testament, in any apostolic-age practice, or in any Reformation-era practice. The historic Reformed conversion-pattern is preaching of the Word, conviction by the Spirit, repentance and faith in the heart, public profession through baptism and church membership over time. Finney's collapse of this pattern into a single physical-public response at the close of the sermon has produced a century and a half of American Evangelicalism that confuses public response with regenerate conversion. Iain Murray's Revival and Revivalism (1994) is the standard Reformed-confessional documentation of the difference. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph rebuts the altar-call innovation by name.
